stem: Haskins says he disliked 'that dry prairie' and missed timber and rain. What larger point does Garland make through Haskins?

stimulus.source_note: Hamlin Garland, 'Under the Lion's Paw,' Main-Travelled Roads (1891). Public domain. Text verified against Project Gutenberg (eBook #2809) and Original Sources.
stimulus.text:
Hamlin Garland, 'Under the Lion's Paw,' in Main-Travelled Roads (1891) (ellipses mark omissions):

"It was the last of autumn and first day of winter coming together. All day long the ploughmen on their prairie farms had moved to and fro in their wide level fields through the falling snow, which melted as it fell, wetting them to the skin all day, notwithstanding the frequent squalls of snow, the dripping, desolate clouds, and the muck of the furrows, black and tenacious as tar."

"'I didn't like the looks of the country, anyhow,' Haskins said. 'I was ust t' northern Ingyannie, where we have lots o' timber 'n' lots o' rain, 'n' I didn't like the looks o' that dry prairie.'"

options.text: The Plains punished farmers who brought eastern expectations to a dry land
The Plains rewarded anyone willing to work hard enough
options.misconception: Background: Haskins worked hard and was still driven out by grasshoppers and debt; two-thirds of homesteaders failed.

options.text: Farmers failed because they refused to plant trees
options.misconception: Background: Haskins's troubles were grasshoppers, drought, and debt, not a refusal to plant trees.

options.text: The government gave Haskins land that was too small to farm
options.misconception: Background: the Homestead Act gave 160 acres; Haskins's trouble in the story is grasshoppers, debt, and the mortgage, not the size of the claim.

rationales.A: Haskins came from wet, timbered Indiana. Background: the dry prairie ate his crops and his savings, and the books agree the Plains broke farmers who farmed them as if they were the East, and two-thirds of homesteaders gave up.
rationales.B: Background: Haskins worked hard and was still driven out by grasshoppers and debt, and two-thirds of homesteaders failed.
rationales.C: Background: Haskins's troubles were grasshoppers, drought, and debt, not a refusal to plant trees.
rationales.D: Background: the Homestead Act gave 160 acres, and Haskins's trouble in the story is grasshoppers, debt, and the mortgage, not the size of the claim.
rationales.general:
Picture a farmer from rainy Indiana, standing on a dry Kansas prairie that will not grow what he knows.
1. Hear what Haskins misses. Timber and rain, the things his old home gave freely.
2. Hear what the prairie gives instead. Background: Dry soil, grasshoppers, and a mortgage that outlives the crop.
3. Name Garland's point. The land itself defeated farmers who farmed it like the East.
Remember: a new country punishes old habits, and the punishment lands on the farmer, not the habit.
